_WHY_SERIALISED_AND_NOT_GIVEN_ITS_OWN_CO: THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG ONE AND THE RULING SAYS SO. A lane found that both units default to CPUSET="${A1WRT_CPUSET:-10}", so two rows enqueued together would collide on core 10, and the launcher's G-OCC RECORDS AND QUEUES BUT NEVER REFUSES -- it would not stop the collision. The apparent repair is to set A1WRT_CPUSET to a second core for U2. THAT IS REFUSED. U1 and U2 EXIST TO BE COMPARED -- that comparison IS the item, and its whole claim is to be one-variable. Running the two arms on different cores makes CPU PLACEMENT a variable that differs between them, and this family already carries G12_cpu_placement_F-P GATE FAIL on record: placement is demonstrably not free in these measurements. Solving a scheduling collision by splitting the arms would buy throughput by spending the very thing the item exists to measure. THE SHARED CPUSET DEFAULT IS NOT A DEFECT TO ROUTE AROUND -- IT IS THE ONE-VARIABLE DESIGN EXPRESSING ITSELF, and the collision is the reason to SERIALISE, not the reason to split. Both arms therefore run on core 10, sequentially, on identical placement. Serialising is also what CLOSES the G-OCC gap, rather than relying on a guard that reports and does not refuse.
